fetched_contents.text: Anaerobic degradation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons ABSTRACT Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are ubiquitous and toxic pollutants in the environment that are mostly introduced through anthropogenic activities. They are very stable with low bioavailability and, because aerobic degradation is mostly limited in aquifers and sediments, often persist in anoxic systems. In this review, we elucidate the recent advances in PAH degradation by anaerobic, mostly sulfate-reducing cultures. The best-studied compound is naphthalene, the smallest and simplest PAH, which often serves as a model compound for anaerobic PAH degradation. In recent years, three-ring PAHs have also shifted into focus, using phenanthrene as a representative compound. Anaerobic degradation of PAHs has to overcome several biochemical problems. First, non-substituted PAHs have to be activated by carboxylation, which is chemically challenging and proposed to involve a 1,3-cycloaddition with a UbiD-like carboxylase and a prenylated flavin cofactor. The second key reaction is to overcome the resonance energy of the ring system, which is performed by consecutive two-electron reduction steps involving novel type III aryl-CoA reductases belonging to the old-yellow enzyme family. In naphthalene degradation, a type I aryl-CoA reductase is also involved in reducing a benzene ring structure. The third key reaction is the ring cleavage, involving β-oxidation-like reactions in cleaving ring I of naphthalene. Ring II, however, is opened by a novel lyase reaction at a tertiary, hydroxylated carbon atom. These principles are explained using examples of anaerobic naphthalene and phenanthrene degradation to give an overview of recent advances, from the initial activation of the molecules to the complete degradation to CO2. KEYWORDS: PAH degradation, anaerobic degradation, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, sulfate-reducing bacteria, bioremediation, environmental microbiology INTRODUCTION Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in the environment Aromatic hydrocarbons are a class of organic pollutants occurring in nearly all environments worldwide and imposing a wide range of negative effects on habitats as well as humans and animals. Practically all aromatic hydrocarbons exhibit adverse health effects, ranging from carcinogenicity and acute toxicity in humans to general toxic and mutagenic effects on all life forms (1–5). Many aromatic compounds occur naturally in the environment in minor amounts, originating from volcanic eruptions and natural oil seeps, or production as metabolites or signaling and defense molecules by some plants, fungi, or a few species of termites (6–9). Anthropogenic point sources where aromatic hydrocarbons are discharged into the environment include landfills, previous industrial sites such as coal gasification factories, leaking pipelines and tanks, and spills during the transport of chemicals or oil. Diffuse sources are mostly associated with the incomplete combustion of wood, fossil fuels, and coal. Such contaminations are widespread and can move with the groundwater flow, and it is practically impossible to totally remove them (10, 11). Aromatic hydrocarbons can be classified into monocyclic hydrocarbons (BTEX—benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylene) and PAHs. PAHs are more diverse, including various aromatic compounds with more than one aromatic ring, for example, naphthalene with two rings or phenanthrene and anthracene with three rings. Naphthalene is often used as a model compound as it is the smallest and simplest PAH. Very little is known about the degradation of PAHs with three or more rings, but the pathways are expected to be very similar to naphthalene degradation. For this reason, the review will focus on naphthalene degradation exemplarily, and the bigger PAHs will be discussed briefly at the end of this manuscript. Most PAHs have a very low water solubility, of which naphthalene exhibits one of the highest, with approximately 0.25 mM at 25°C (12). The water solubility of PAHs decreases with increasing number of aromatic rings. Due to the stability of the molecules with 10 or more delocalized π-electrons, the low water solubility, and the high tendency to adsorb to sediments or soils, the bioavailability of PAHs is low (13–15). Aerobic degradation of aromatics is well studied and will not be addressed in this review (16–18). The most relevant difference between aerobic and anaerobic degradation of aromatic hydrocarbons is the use of oxygenases and molecular oxygen in aerobic microorganisms to activate the molecule by hydroxylating and finally cleaving the aromatic ring. All these reactions are no option in anoxic environments (19). However, oxygen gets quickly depleted during aerobic degradation, and contaminated aquifers and sediments turn anoxic upon small contaminant loads, opening an ecological niche for anaerobic degraders (20). PAHs as carbon and electron source First experiments showing anaerobic degradation of aromatic hydrocarbons were carried out with environmental samples and sewage sludge, but only a few enrichments or pure cultures were obtained (21–27). This could be due to the slow growth of the cultures with doubling times ranging from a few weeks to several months, as well as the small growth yields (20, 28). Sulfate is a common electron acceptor used during anaerobic PAH degradation (22, 23, 29–33), but denitrification (21), methanogenesis (34, 35), and iron reduction (31, 36, 37) have also been shown. The first evidence of anaerobic degradation of naphthalene or higher PAHs under sulfate-reducing conditions was found in soil samples (32, 38). In the same year, carboxylic acids (2-naphthoic acid and 2-phenanthroic acid, respectively) were found as intermediates of naphthalene and phenanthrene degradation in an enrichment culture from contaminated harbor sediment, indicating carboxylation as the initial activation reaction of naphthalene and phenanthrene (22). fetched_contents.text: Bioaugmentation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH)-contaminated soil with the nitrate-reducing bacterium PheN7 under anaerobic condition Highlights * • Remediation efficiency of PAH-contaminated soil was enhanced by the anaerobic bioaugmentation. * • The average removal rates of phenanthrene were 1.73 mg/kg soil·d and 1.48 mg/kg soil·d in BA and BS group. * • PheN7 became the dominant species in the end of the cultivation. * • Enhanced UbiD gene and nitrate reductase gene in bioaugmentation group was revealed by PICRUSt analysis. Abstract The remediation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH)-contaminated soil under anaerobic condition is still a huge challenge. In this study, an anaerobic Bacillus firmus strain named PheN7 was firstly isolated from mixture of contaminated soil and sludge samples with phenanthrene as the sole carbon resource under nitrate reducing environment. The anaerobic strain was then inoculated combining with nitrate into the phenanthrene-spiked PAH-contaminated soil to investigate the remediation efficiency by anaerobic bioaugmentation (BA). Results showed that the synergy between PheN7 and indigenous degrading bacteria promoted the remediation efficiency of soil. The average removal efficiencies of phenanthrene in 56 days were 1.73 mg/kg soil·d in BA group, much higher than biostimulation group (sole nitrate addition) and natural degradation which achieved 1.48 mg/kg soil·d and 1.24 mg/kg soil·d of degradation rate, respectively. The outstanding adaptability of PheN7 made it become the dominant species in soil in the terminal period, but the invasion of PheN7 also resulted in the decline of diversity of the indigenous microbial community. Phylogenetic Investigation of Communities by Reconstruction of Unobserved States 2 (PICRUSt 2) results showed that a series of functional genes encoding anaerobic phenanthrene degradation and nitrate reductase enzymes in soil were remarkably strengthened with the addition of PheN7. This study confirmed the contribution of PheN7 as the anaerobic inoculum in PAH-contaminated soil remediation, further evaluating the practical applicability of anaerobic bioaugmentation technology in on-site remediation of real PAH-contaminated sites. Introduction With the high-speed development of the petroleum industry and the massive usage of fossil fuel products, more than one billion tons of petroleum pollutants are generated worldwide each year (Hu et al., 2013). Petroleum hydrocarbons, halogenated hydrocarbons and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) dominate the pollutant list, in which PAHs have received increasing attention owing to its teratogenicity and carcinogenicity (Samanta et al., 2002). Plenty of lands are now suffering from the heavy pollution of PAHs due to the improper disposal of oily waste (Haritash and Kaushik, 2009, Li et al., 2015). To solve the problem of PAH-contaminated soil, various remediation technologies have been developed in the past few decades, in which eco-friendly microorganism repair technology is one kind of biological remediation techniques that mainly relies on the indigenous PAH-degrading bacteria or foreign microbial inoculum to ultimately realize the degradation of PAHs (Samanta et al., 2002). Bioaugmentation technology refers as the introduction of specific functional microorganism into the targeted environment, which has been successively carried out in the remediation of oil-contaminated soil (Wu et al., 2016). The inoculum generally comes from the foreign bacteria (Michalsen et al., 2016) or the isolated indigenous bacterial consortium (Lu et al., 2019). Once getting into the soil, the activity of foreign bacteria would be affected by both abiotic and biotic factors (Chen et al., 2022). For instance, the absence of oxygen in deep soil could inhibit the activity of inoculated aerobic bacteria, weakening the removal efficiency of organic pollutants and making deep soil a gathering layer of persistent organic contamination (Mohan et al., 2006). Bioventing was generally used to overcome this adversity by introducing oxygen or air into the deep soil while increasing the cost of the restoration (Hussain et al., 2022). Under this circumstance, the introduction of foreign anaerobic degrading bacteria was theoretically effective in removing organic pollutant in deep site of soil (Zhao et al., 2022). Actually, anaerobic bioaugmentation technology have been tentatively applied in the remediation of oil refinery sludge (Roy et al., 2018) and hexahydro-1,3,5-trinitro-1,3,5-triazine (RDX)-contaminated groundwater plume (Michalsen et al., 2020). But this technology still developed in a slow speed since the short of anaerobic degrading bacteria and the dicey adaptability of foreign inoculum in real contaminated soil. The isolation of PAH-degrading bacteria has been conducted since the last century. More than 100 kinds of aerobic PAH-degrading strains or enriched cultures have been achieved thus far, the related degrading mechanisms have also been thoroughly studied (Ghosal et al., 2016). However, the isolation of anaerobic PAH-degrading bacteria is still limited on account of the strict environmental requirements and long degradation cycles. Moreover, the biodegradability of the isolated anaerobic bacteria was mainly restricted to low molecular weight (LMW) PAHs (less than 3 benzene rings) (Galushko et al., 1999, Zhang et al., 2019). So far, several phenanthrene-degrading bacteria were isolated under anaerobic condition, including Achromobacter with nitrate as the electron acceptor (Zhang et al., 2021b), and Trichococcus alkaliphilus with Fe(Ⅲ) as the electron acceptor (Zhang et al., 2021a). fetched_contents.text: Enhanced anoxic biodegradation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in a highly contaminated aged soil using nitrate and soil microbes Enhanced anoxic biodegradation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in a highly contaminated aged soil using nitrate and soil microbes Yang, S; Gou, Y; Song, Yun; Li, P Reference Type Journal Article HERO ID 6913232 In Press No Year 2018 Title Enhanced anoxic biodegradation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in a highly contaminated aged soil using nitrate and soil microbes Authors Yang, S; Gou, Y; Song, Yun; Li, P Journal Environmental Earth Sciences Volume 77 Issue 12 Page Numbers 1-11 Abstract Biodegradation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) is an alternative method for the removal of these compounds from polluted environments. However, there is a lack of knowledge regarding anoxic degradation of the 16 United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) priority PAHs by indigenous bacteria in a highly contaminated aged soil with PAHs. Accordingly, we hypothesized that nitrate, as an electron acceptor, can enhance the anoxic biodegradation of PAHs in the presence of soil microbes, in contaminated soils. The objective was to investigate if the use of nitrate and soil microbes can enhance the anoxic biodegradation of PAHs in an aged soil from a former steel-making factory. The addition of nitrate did not improve the anoxic biodegradation of 5- and 6-ring PAHs; however, it facilitated anoxic biodegradation of 3- and 4-ring PAHs in soil (p < 0.05). After 300 days of anoxic incubation, the removal efficiency of 3- and 4-ring PAHs ranged from 45 to 73% and 32–63%, respectively. As more nitrate was added, the percentage of 3- and 4-ring PAHs biodegraded increased. Bacteria capable of degrading PAHs under anoxic conditions were dominated by bacterial strains belonging to Proteobacteria and Firmicutes, which accounted for 55% of the total number of indigenous bacteria in soil. Moreover, the total number of Proteobacteria and Firmicutes increased with nitrate added, facilitating the degradation of 3- and 4-ring PAHs. The results in this study also showed that the recalcitrance of PAHs increased with increasing number of benzene rings, molecular weight and organic carbon/water partition coefficient (Koc) of PAHs. However, the recalcitrance of PAHs increased with decreasing solubility of the PAHs. Overall, the results of this study offer an attractive approach to the removal of PAHs from polluted subsurface soils in industrial sites using nitrate and the consortium of soil bacteria. Nitrates alone appear to function primarily as electron acceptors rather than cometabolic substrates in anaerobic PAH degradation. The background review states that sulfate is a common electron acceptor used during anaerobic PAH degradation, but denitrification, methanogenesis, and iron reduction have also been shown, and nitrate as an electron acceptor has been repeatedly observed in environmental samples and microcosm experiments [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The same review explicitly identifies nitrate-reducing, denitrifying, iron-reducing, sulfate-reducing, methanogenic, and anoxygenic phototrophic organisms as linked to aromatic degradation [N1-R4]. This means that nitrates are most plausibly acting as electron acceptors, supporting denitrifying metabolism rather than serving as a direct cometabolic carbon source.

On which PAHs are degraded more or less under nitrate addition, the evidence is mixed but suggestive. The experimental study on aged soil showed that nitrate addition did not improve anoxic biodegradation of 5- and 6-ring PAHs, but it did facilitate anoxic biodegradation of 3- and 4-ring PAHs [N5-F3]. This indicates that nitrate addition tends to enhance degradation of smaller, less recalcitrant PAHs, while having little or no effect on larger, more recalcitrant PAHs. The review also emphasizes that the recalcitrance of PAHs increases with the number of benzene rings, molecular weight, and organic carbon/water partition coefficient (Koc), but decreases with solubility [N5-F3]. So, under nitrate addition, the pattern is likely: higher degradation for 3- and 4-ring PAHs, and lower or neutral for 5- and 6-ring PAHs.

Regarding degradation rates and pathway intermediates, the review provides a detailed mechanistic picture. It explains that anaerobic PAH degradation involves initial activation by carboxylation, followed by consecutive two-electron reduction steps involving type III aryl-CoA reductases from the old-yellow enzyme family, and ring cleavage by β-oxidation-like reactions or novel lyase reactions [N1-F1]. The review also notes that these pathways differ from aerobic degradation, which relies on oxygenases and molecular oxygen [N1-F1]. The experimental study on aged soil does not specify intermediates directly, but it does show that the addition of nitrate increased the total number of Proteobacteria and Firmicutes, and facilitated degradation of 3- and 4-ring PAHs [N5-F3]. This suggests that nitrate addition can alter the microbial community and thus shift the overall pathway environment, possibly favoring pathways that are more active under denitrifying conditions.

In short: nitrates serve as electron acceptors in anaerobic PAH degradation [N1-F1][N1-R4], they tend to enhance degradation of smaller 3- and 4-ring PAHs more than larger 5- and 6-ring PAHs [N5-F3], and they can change the microbial community and apparent pathway environment, with little evidence in the provided material that they function as cometabolic substrates [N1-F1][N1-R4].

Bacillus firmus appears to be a relevant anaerobic PAH-degrading microorganism, but the evidence points more strongly to its role in bioaugmentation and microbial community dynamics than to a complete mechanistic pathway description. The direct experimental study on anaerobic bioaugmentation with PheN7, an anaerobic Bacillus firmus strain isolated under nitrate-reducing conditions, showed that inoculation with PheN7 improved PAH-contaminated soil remediation, especially phenanthrene removal [N2-F2]. It also reported that PheN7 became the dominant species in the terminal period and that functional genes for anaerobic phenanthrene degradation and nitrate reductase were enhanced by bioaugmentation [N2-F2]. This indicates that Bacillus firmus can contribute PAH-degradation activity under anaerobic conditions and that it may carry out nitrate-dependent electron transport pathways.

The specific PAH-degrading enzymes or pathways used by Bacillus firmus are only partially described in the provided evidence. The study on anthracene degradation by Bacillus firmus mentions membrane-protein dynamics during anthracene biodegradation, suggesting that membrane-associated enzymes are involved in the process [N2-R3]. However, the evidence does not give a full biochemical pathway for Bacillus firmus, so any claim about a precise enzyme set must be cautious. The broader anaerobic PAH review describes general activation by carboxylation and two-electron reduction steps involving type III aryl-CoA reductases and ring cleavage reactions, but it does not tie those enzymes specifically to Bacillus firmus [N1-F1]. Therefore, the safest conclusion is that the evidence supports the role of membrane-associated proteins and denitrifying/nitrate-reductase-linked metabolism, but not a complete enzyme catalog [N2-R3][N2-F2].

As for whether nitrates enhance or inhibit microbial activity and degradation, the evidence is mixed but overall favorable. The direct bioaugmentation study found that the synergy between PheN7 and indigenous degrading bacteria promoted remediation efficiency, and that the addition of PheN7 increased functional genes associated with anaerobic phenanthrene degradation and nitrate reductase [N2-F2]. It also showed that the average removal rate in the bioaugmentation group was much higher than in the biostimulation-only nitrate addition group and natural degradation [N2-F2]. In the aged soil experiment, nitrate addition increased the total number of Proteobacteria and Firmicutes and facilitated degradation of 3- and 4-ring PAHs, suggesting that nitrates can enhance microbial activity and degradation under the right conditions [N5-F3]. However, the same aged soil study also shows that nitrate addition had no effect on 5- and 6-ring PAHs, indicating that the enhancement is context-dependent rather than universal [N5-F3].

The community-shift effects are clearly documented. In the bioaugmentation study, PheN7 became the dominant species in the terminal period, and its addition reduced indigenous microbial diversity [N2-F2]. In the aged soil experiment, nitrate addition increased the abundance of Proteobacteria and Firmicutes, indicating a shift in dominant taxa [N5-F3]. These shifts can have important consequences for overall PAH removal: the bioaugmentation study suggests that the dominant inoculum can drive high removal rates, while the aged soil study suggests that nitrate addition can favor broader community changes that support degradation of 3- and 4-ring PAHs [N2-F2][N5-F3]. However, the evidence also notes that the invasion of PheN7 reduced indigenous diversity, which may weaken long-term resilience or persistence [N2-F2]. In short, Bacillus firmus can enhance PAH removal under anaerobic conditions, especially when paired with nitrate addition, but the response depends on the PAH size class and the microbial community structure [N2-F2][N5-F3].
